original_value: Wilderness search and rescue (WSAR) requires careful communication between workers in different locations. To understand the contexts from which WSAR workers communicate and the challenges they face, we interviewed WSAR workers and observed a mock-WSAR scenario. Our findings illustrate that WSAR workers face challenges in maintaining a shared mental model. This is primarily done through distributed communication using two-way radios and cell phones for text and photo messaging; yet both implicit and explicit communication suffer. WSAR workers send messages for various reasons and share different types of information with varying levels of urgency. This warrants the use of multiple communication modalities and information streams. However, bringing in more modalities introduces the risk of information overload, and thus WSAR workers today still primarily communicate remotely via the radio. Our work demonstrates opportunities for technology to provide implicit communication and awareness remotely, and to help teams maintain a shared mental model even when synchronous realtime communication is sparse. Furthermore, technology should be designed to bring together multiple streams of information and communication while making sure that they are presented in ways that aid WSAR workers rather than overwhelming them.

result.paraphrase: Wilderness search and rescue (WSAR) depends on careful coordination among workers in different locations. To learn about the settings from which WSAR workers communicate and the difficulties they encounter, we interviewed WSAR workers and observed a mock WSAR scenario. Our findings show that WSAR workers struggle to maintain a shared mental model. This is mainly achieved through distributed communication with two-way radios and cell phones for text and photo messaging, yet both implicit and explicit communication are affected. WSAR workers send messages for many reasons and exchange different kinds of information with varying urgency. This calls for multiple communication modalities and information streams. But adding more modalities can create information overload, so WSAR workers still mainly communicate remotely by radio. Our work points to opportunities for technology to support remote implicit communication and awareness, and to help teams preserve a shared mental model even when synchronous real-time communication is limited. In addition, technology should combine multiple streams of information and communication while presenting them in ways that help WSAR workers rather than overwhelm them.
